extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in U.S. politics, media coverage, and free-speech/legal implications
extracted.subtask_description: A news/Wikipedia-style compilation summarizing media, political, legal, and public reactions to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, including employer discipline, political responses, and relevant U.S. case law on free speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickering v. Board of Education (1968) — public employee speech standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under case law in the United States, such as Pickering v. Board of Education (1968), it was established that public employees including teachers have the right to free speech on matters of public concern without termination, excluding any statements that are "knowingly" or "recklessly false".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in assessing whether disciplining or firing public employees for off-duty speech violates the First Amendment; the exception for knowingly or recklessly false statements is a limiting principle cited in employer-termination disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garcetti v. Ceballos (2006) — speech made as agency representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Garcetti v. Ceballos (2006) affirms that First Amendment protections are not given for any public employee comments made as representatives for their agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to distinguish speech protected as private-public commentary from speech made in an official capacity; relevant when evaluating whether a public employee's statements are constitutionally protected or subject to employer discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969) — disruption test for school-related speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969) restricts the protections if the actions or speech would interfere or disrupt the school's operation or infringe on others' rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess limits on student/educator speech in educational settings—if speech causes substantial disruption or infringes others' rights, First Amendment protection may be limited.
